Guilty
gĭlt´y
adj. (chargeable with an offence, liable to penalty; rendering Hebrew asham, Greek hupodikos, enochos)
From Anglo-Saxon gylt, a fault, crime, debt. The English word keeps the debt-sense that Scripture's trespass-offering assumes: guilt is something owed.

Biblical Definition

Guilty in Scripture is objective liability, not a feeling. Leviticus makes this unmistakable: a man may sin through ignorance, with the matter hidden from his own eyes, “though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity” (Lev 5:17). Guilt is a status before God's law, incurred whether or not the conscience has caught up. Joseph's brothers show the reverse case — the awakening of a guilt long carried: “We are verily guilty concerning our brother” (Gen 42:21), spoken twenty years after the deed. The divine character holds both mercy and this refusal together in one breath: the LORD forgives iniquity and transgression and sin, “and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exo 34:7) — a sentence that makes the cross necessary, since God will neither leave the guilty unpunished nor abandon those He pardons. Paul's summary closes every mouth: “all the world may become guilty before God” (Rom 3:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines guilty as justly chargeable with a crime, criminal, and notes that in Scripture the word signifies liability to punishment, not merely the consciousness of wrong.

expand to see more

GUILT´Y, a. Justly chargeable with a crime; not innocent.

2. Wicked; corrupt; sinful.

3. Conscious of guilt; as a guilty look.

In Scripture, guilty often signifies exposed to punishment; liable to the penalty of the law.

Key Scripture

Rom 3:19 — "Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God."

Exo 34:7 — "Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation."

Lev 5:17 — "And if a soul sin, and commit any of these things which are forbidden to be done by the commandments of the LORD; though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity."

Gen 42:21 — "And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear; therefore is this distress come upon us."

Modern Corruption

Guilt reclassified as a psychological injury to be relieved rather than a legal status to be pardoned — so that the gospel's answer is offered to a problem the age no longer believes it has.

expand to see more

The therapeutic settlement treats guilt as a feeling that damages self-worth, and therefore as something to be dissolved by reframing. On that account, forgiveness is a technique for feeling better and the cross is at best a symbol of acceptance. Scripture's guilt cannot be reframed, because Leviticus 5:17 establishes that a man is guilty whether or not he knows it. A status incurred by objective violation cannot be talked away by a change in self-perception; it must be borne, either by the sinner or by a substitute.

Yet false guilt is also real, and the same doctrine cures it. Where guilt is objective, it can be objectively answered: the believer is not asked to feel less guilty but to look away from himself to a finished work. Exodus 34:7 will not clear the guilty — and that is precisely why the guilty may be cleared, since at the cross the penalty was exacted rather than waived. God did not lower the standard; He satisfied it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asham (H816), to be guilty, to incur liability — the root of the trespass-offering; Greek hupodikos (G5267), liable to judgment, literally under the sentence, in Rom 3:19.

expand to see more

Hebrew asham (H816) — to be guilty, to bear punishment; the same root names the guilt-offering, so guilt and its remedy share a word.

Greek hupodikos (G5267) — under judgment, answerable to a court; Paul's verdict on the whole world (Rom 3:19).

Greek enochos (G1777) — held in, liable; used of one guilty of the body and blood of the Lord (1Co 11:27).

Usage

"“Though he wist it not, yet is he guilty” — guilt is a status, not a sensation."

"“That will by no means clear the guilty” — the sentence that makes substitution necessary."

"“All the world may become guilty before God” — every mouth stopped."
